title: Past Tense
plainEnglish: Shows that an action or state already happened or is finished.
whenToUse: Reach for this whenever the event is over: a completed action (어제 영화를 봤어요 = I watched a movie yesterday), a past state (어제는 바빴어요 = I was busy yesterday), or a result you can still feel now (밥을 먹었어요 = I've eaten / I'm full). It is also the natural answer to 뭐 했어요? (What did you do?). Korean does not separate simple past from present perfect the way English does, so this single ending covers both 'I ate' and 'I have eaten'; let context decide. Stack a time word in front (어제, 아까, 지난주) and the past meaning becomes unmistakable: 지난주에 친구를 만났어요 (I met a friend last week).
attachmentRule: Drop 다 from the stem. If the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 았어요 (가다→갔어요, 좋다→좋았어요). Otherwise add 었어요 (먹다→먹었어요, 마시다→마셨어요). 하다 verbs become 했어요 (공부하다→공부했어요). Irregular stems shift: ㄷ irregular 듣다→들었어요, ㅂ irregular 춥다→추웠어요, ㅡ drops 바쁘다→바빴어요.
contrastWith: Don't confuse the finished past V-았/었어요 with the experiential V-(으)ㄴ 적 있다. 어제 김치를 먹었어요 reports one concrete event (I ate kimchi yesterday), while 김치를 먹은 적 있어요 asks/states only whether it has *ever* happened in your life (I've eaten kimchi before), with no specific time. Also separate it from present V-아/어요: 지금 먹어요 (I'm eating now) vs 아까 먹었어요 (I ate a moment ago). A subtle trap: 결혼했어요 looks past but often means the present state 'I am married', because the change happened once and still holds — Korean uses the past form for such resulting states.

examples.en: I slept yesterday.
I ate bread and drank coffee in the morning.

examples.ko: 주말에 친구를 만나서 영화를 봤는데 정말 재미있었어요.
examples.en: I met a friend on the weekend and we saw a movie, and it was really fun.
The weather was really cold yesterday.

commonMistakes: Choosing 았어요 after a vowel that is not ㅏ/ㅗ: ❌먹았어요. Why: vowel harmony picks 았 only after the bright ㅏ/ㅗ; 먹 has ㅓ, so the dark-vowel ending is required → ✅먹었어요. Listen to the stem vowel, not the meaning.
Treating 하다 like a regular stem: ❌하았어요 / ❌하었어요. Why: 하다 is special and always contracts → ✅했어요, so 공부하다→공부했어요, 운동하다→운동했어요. Memorize 했어요 as a fixed shape.
Adding a separate word for 'have' as in English: ❌먹었어요 있어요 for 'I have eaten'. Why: Korean has no 'have + past participle'; the one ending 먹었어요 already means both 'I ate' and 'I have eaten'.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Check if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ
Add 았어요 or 었어요, or use 했어요 for 하다
Apply irregular changes if the stem is irregular
beginnerExplanation: Think of the past tense as one decision: bright or dark. After you drop 다, look at the last vowel of the stem — if it is the 'bright' ㅏ or ㅗ, the ending stays bright too (았어요), so 가다→갔어요 (I went) and 좋다→좋았어요 (it was good). Every other vowel is treated as 'dark' and takes 었어요, so 먹다→먹었어요 (I ate). A handy mnemonic: ㅏ and ㅗ are the two vowels with a stroke pointing right/up, the 'sunny' side, and sunny stems keep the sunny 았. The one rule-breaker you must simply memorize is 하다 → 했어요, never 하았어요. And unlike English, Korean does not bolt on a helper verb for 'have done' — the same 먹었어요 carries both 'I ate' and 'I have eaten', so once vowel harmony is automatic, this is one of the easiest endings in the language.

title: Future / Intention
plainEnglish: Expresses a future plan, an intention, or a guess about what will happen.
whenToUse: Use it for three closely related jobs: a plan or schedule (내일 부산에 갈 거예요 = I'm going to Busan tomorrow), a personal decision or intention (저는 한국어를 공부할 거예요 = I'm going to study Korean), and a guess about something you can't see for certain (지금 집에 없을 거예요 = he's probably not home right now). Add 아마 (probably) to lean into the guessing sense. It answers 내일 뭐 할 거예요? (What are you going to do tomorrow?) naturally. Because it states a neutral plan rather than making a promise to the listener, it is the safe, all-purpose 'will/be going to' for everyday conversation.
attachmentRule: Drop 다 from the stem. After a vowel-ending stem add ㄹ 거예요 (가다→갈 거예요, 보다→볼 거예요). After a consonant-ending stem add 을 거예요 (먹다→먹을 거예요, 읽다→읽을 거예요). ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ and take ㄹ 거예요 (살다→살 거예요). ㅂ irregular: 돕다→도울 거예요; ㄷ irregular: 듣다→들을 거예요.
contrastWith: Don't confuse V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 with V-(으)ㄹ게요. Both point to the future, but 거예요 states a plan as neutral information (주말에 집에 있을 거예요 = I'll be home this weekend, just telling you), while 게요 makes a real-time promise/offer *to* the listener, usually reacting to them (제가 할게요 = I'll do it — don't worry). You cannot use 게요 for a third person or for weather: ❌내일 비가 올게요; you must say 올 거예요. Also separate it from present V-아/어요, which is current action, not a plan. Quick test: if you're volunteering in response to someone, use 게요; if you're just reporting what will happen, use 거예요.

examples.en: I'm going to sleep.
I'll read a book in the evening.

examples.ko: 주말에 친구를 만날 건데 같이 갈래요?
examples.en: I'm going to meet a friend this weekend — do you want to come along?
It will probably rain tomorrow.

commonMistakes: Adding 을 거예요 after a vowel stem: ❌갈을 거예요. Why: a vowel stem already supplies the ㄹ, so you only attach the bare ㄹ 거예요 → ✅갈 거예요. The 을 is only for consonant stems (먹을 거예요).
Misspelling the ending as 거에요: ❌갈 거에요. Why: it is 거 (the noun 것) + 예요 (the polite copula after a vowel) → ✅거예요. They sound nearly identical, but only 거예요 is correct.
Using 거예요 to make a promise to someone: ❌(to a worried friend) 제가 도와줄 거예요. Why: that states a neutral plan and sounds detached; to reassure the listener use the promising ending → ✅제가 도와줄게요.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Check if the stem ends in a vowel or a consonant
Add ㄹ 거예요 after a vowel or 을 거예요 after a consonant
Handle ㄹ-stems and irregular stems
beginnerExplanation: This is your everyday 'will / be going to', and it doubles as a soft guess when you're not sure. The shape splits purely by sound: a vowel-ending stem just adds the consonant ㄹ (가다→갈 거예요 = I'll go), while a consonant-ending stem needs a little 을 bridge first (먹다→먹을 거예요 = I'll eat). Picture 거 as the noun 'thing/the case' — literally you're saying 'going is the plan', which is why the same form slides into a prediction: 아마 비가 올 거예요 = 'rain coming is probably the case' (it'll probably rain). The number-one beginner trap is spelling: write 거예요, not 거에요. And don't reach for it when you're promising something to a person in front of you — that job belongs to -(으)ㄹ게요.

title: Progressive (be ~ing)
plainEnglish: Shows that an action is happening right now and is still going on.
whenToUse: Use it to zoom in on an action unfolding at this very moment (지금 밥을 먹고 있어요 = I'm eating right now), or for an ongoing activity over a stretch of time even if you're not doing it this second (요즘 한국어를 배우고 있어요 = I'm learning Korean these days). It's the natural reply to 지금 뭐 하고 있어요? (What are you doing right now?). With a respected subject, swap 있어요 for 계세요 (선생님이 기다리고 계세요 = the teacher is waiting). Note one quirk: with 'wear' verbs (입다, 신다, 쓰다) 입고 있어요 usually means the resulting *state* 'is wearing' rather than the act of putting on.
attachmentRule: Simply attach 고 있어요 to the plain verb stem with no vowel change at all; the stem ending in a vowel or a consonant makes no difference (가다→가고 있어요, 먹다→먹고 있어요, 공부하다→공부하고 있어요). For respect toward the subject, 있어요 becomes 계세요 (기다리고 계세요).
contrastWith: Don't confuse the action-in-progress V-고 있어요 with the resulting-state V-아/어 있어요. 문을 닫고 있어요 means someone is in the middle of closing the door (the action is happening), while 문이 닫혀 있어요 means the door stands closed (the result remains) — same English 'is closed' but very different Korean. Also separate it from the plain present V-아/어요, which can state a habit or general fact: 저는 커피를 마셔요 can mean 'I drink coffee (generally)', whereas 저는 커피를 마시고 있어요 pins it to right now. Use 고 있어요 only when the ongoing action itself is the point.

examples.en: He's sleeping right now.
My younger sibling is listening to music in their room.

examples.ko: 엄마가 부엌에서 요리하고 계셔서 집에 좋은 냄새가 나요.
examples.en: Mom is cooking in the kitchen, so the house smells great.
I'm waiting for a friend.

commonMistakes: Inserting a connective vowel before 고: ❌먹어고 있어요 / ❌가아고 있어요. Why: 고 clips straight onto the bare stem with no harmony → ✅먹고 있어요, ✅가고 있어요. If you hear yourself adding 어/아, delete it.
Using plain present when the moment matters: saying 먹어요 to mean 'I'm eating right now'. Why: 먹어요 can read as a habit; to stress the action in progress choose ✅먹고 있어요.
Keeping 있어요 for an honored subject: ❌할머니가 주무시고 있어요... with plain 있어요 for the helper. Why: respect the subject by lifting the helper verb too → ✅기다리고 계세요 (and the verb itself: 주무시고 계세요).
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Attach 고 with no vowel change
Add 있어요 to mean is in progress
Switch 있어요 to 계세요 to respect the subject
beginnerExplanation: V-고 있어요 is Korean's 'be ~ing', and the best news for a beginner is that it never changes shape with the verb — no vowel harmony, no exceptions. You simply glue 고 있어요 onto the bare stem: 먹다→먹고 있어요 (I'm eating), 가다→가고 있어요 (I'm going). Think of 고 as a tiny clip and 있어요 ('exist') as 'is currently' — together: 'the eating exists right now'. It earns its keep by contrast: 먹어요 on its own can drift into 'I eat (in general)', but 먹고 있어요 nails the action to this exact moment. The classic slip is reflexively sticking 어/아 before 고 (producing 먹어고); resist it — 고 loves the naked stem. One thing to watch later: with clothing verbs, 입고 있어요 leans toward 'is wearing' (a state), not 'is putting on'.

title: Try Doing
plainEnglish: Means to try doing something or to give something a go.
whenToUse: Use it in two everyday situations. First, to warmly suggest someone attempt an action — 이거 한번 먹어 보세요 (give this a try) — where adding 한번 ('once / just') makes the invitation feel light and low-pressure. Second, in the past tense to talk about an experience you've had a go at: 제주도에 가 봤어요 (I've been to Jeju / I tried going to Jeju). Because 보다 literally means 'see', the nuance is 'do it and see how it goes', so it's perfect for recommending food, clothes to try on, places to visit, or new methods. You then conjugate the 보다 part for whatever tense you need: 보세요 (please try), 봤어요 (tried), 볼 거예요 (will try).
attachmentRule: Take the 아/어 connective like in present tense. If the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ use 아 보다 (가다→가 보다, 찾다→찾아 보다); otherwise use 어 보다 (먹다→먹어 보다, 입다→입어 보다). 하다 becomes 해 보다. Then conjugate 보다 normally: 보세요 (please try), 봤어요 (tried), 볼 거예요 (will try).
contrastWith: Don't confuse 'try *doing*' V-아/어 보다 with 'try *to* do / attempt with effort' V-(으)려고 하다. 한국어로 말해 봤어요 means 'I gave speaking Korean a go / I had a try at it' (and likely succeeded enough to see), while 한국어로 말하려고 했어요 means 'I was trying/intending to speak Korean' (with the attempt possibly failing or being interrupted). Also separate it from the bare verb: 먹어요 is just 'eat', but 먹어 봐요 adds 'eat it and see'. A spelling note: the experiential past is 가 봤어요, but the *existence* of an experience is 가 본 적 있어요 — different grammar, often confused.

examples.en: Try it on.

examples.ko: 이 김치가 매운데 한번 먹어 보세요.
examples.en: This kimchi is spicy, but give it a try.

examples.ko: 저는 제주도에 가 봤는데 바다가 정말 예뻤어요.
examples.en: I've been to Jeju, and the sea was really beautiful.

examples.ko: 다음에 한국 음식을 직접 만들어 볼 거예요.
examples.en: Next time I'm going to try making Korean food myself.

commonMistakes: Picking the wrong connective vowel: ❌먹아 보세요. Why: 먹 has the dark vowel ㅓ, so the connective must be 어 → ✅먹어 보세요. Only ㅏ/ㅗ stems take 아 (가 보다, 찾아 보다).
Leaving 보다 unconjugated: ❌먹어 보 / ❌먹어 보다 (as a finished sentence). Why: 보다 still needs a real ending → ✅먹어 보세요 (please try) or ✅먹어 봤어요 (I tried). Always finish the 보- part.

Confusing 'try and see' with 'see/watch': writing 보다 as a separate literal 'look'. Why: here 보다 is a helper meaning 'and see how it goes', not '(physically) look at'; ✅이거 먹어 보세요 = 'taste this', not 'look at eating this'.
studyOrder: Make the 아/어 connective using vowel harmony
Attach 보다 after the connective
Conjugate 보다 for the tense you need
Use 보세요 to gently suggest trying
beginnerExplanation: V-아/어 보다 layers the idea of 'try / experience' on top of any action verb, and it's built from the very same 아/어 connective you already use for the present tense — so if you can make 먹어요, you can make 먹어 보다. The mental image is literal: 보다 means 'see', so 먹어 보다 is 'eat and see', i.e. 'give eating a try'. From there you simply bend the 보- part for the moment you need: the gentle suggestion 먹어 보세요 ('go on, taste it'), or the experience 가 봤어요 ('I've tried going / I've been'), which is how Koreans naturally talk about places they've visited. Adding 한번 ('just once') up front makes any suggestion feel friendly and pressure-free. The most common stumble is stopping at 보 — always carry the ending through to 보세요 or 봤어요.

title: Mild Surprise
plainEnglish: Expresses mild surprise or a fresh realization about something you just noticed.
whenToUse: Use it the instant you notice or learn something and want to react out loud — like an English 'oh!', 'wow', or 'huh, so it is': 날씨가 정말 좋네요 (wow, the weather's really nice), 한국어를 잘하시네요 (oh, you're good at Korean!). It shines when you're responding to what's right in front of you (food, weather, a view, someone's skill) or to news you just heard. Because it carries warmth and a touch of admiration, it's a friendly way to compliment or to show you're engaged. For a reaction about something already finished, use the past 았/었네요: 벌써 다 끝났네요 (oh, it's all done already). It signals 'I'm noticing this now', so it feels spontaneous, not pre-planned.
attachmentRule: Attach 네요 directly to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel harmony (좋다→좋네요, 가다→가네요, 크다→크네요). ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ before 네요 (멀다→머네요, 살다→사네요). For past reactions use 았/었네요 (왔네요, 먹었네요).
contrastWith: Don't confuse the 'I just noticed' A/V-네요 with the 'as you know, right?' A/V-지요(죠). 맛있네요 means you've *just* discovered it's delicious and are reacting freshly, while 맛있죠? assumes the listener already agrees and seeks confirmation ('it's tasty, isn't it?'). Same adjective, opposite stance: 네요 is new information to you; 죠 is shared, expected information. Also separate it from the plain report A/V-아/어요: 비가 와요 simply states 'it's raining', but 비가 오네요 adds 'oh, it's raining (I just noticed)'. If there's no element of fresh discovery, plain 아/어요 is enough.

examples.en: Oh, it's raining.
Wow, this place's kimchi stew is really delicious.

examples.ko: 벌써 시간이 이렇게 됐네요. 빨리 가야겠어요.
examples.en: Oh, it's gotten this late already. I'd better hurry.
You really speak Korean well!

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before 네요: ❌좋아네요 / ❌맛있어네요. Why: 네요 clips straight onto the plain stem with no 아/어 → ✅좋네요, ✅맛있네요.
Keeping ㄹ in ㄹ-stems: ❌멀네요 / ❌살네요. Why: ㄹ drops before ㄴ-initial endings → ✅머네요 (it's far), ✅사네요 (oh, he lives here). This ㄹ-drop is a reliable Korean sound rule.

Using 네요 for old, shared facts: reacting with 네요 to something both speakers already know. Why: 네요 means 'news to me right now'; if it's mutual knowledge, you likely want ✅-지요/죠 (서울은 크죠? = Seoul's big, right?).
studyOrder: Find the plain stem by dropping 다
Attach 네요 directly with no vowel change
Drop ㄹ first if the stem ends in ㄹ
Use 았/었네요 for a reaction about the past
beginnerExplanation: A/V-네요 is the little 'oh!' / 'wow' ending Koreans sprinkle through conversation the moment something strikes them. Mechanically it's a gift: attach 네요 straight onto the stem with zero vowel harmony, so 좋다→좋네요 (oh, nice) and 맛있다→맛있네요 (wow, tasty). The feeling it adds is fresh discovery — you're noticing this right now and saying so, which is why it lands as warm, even admiring, when you aim it at someone's cooking or skill (잘하시네요!). Think of it as the spoken equivalent of raised eyebrows. Two things trip beginners up: don't slip 아/어 in before 네요, and remember the sound rule that ㄹ-stems lose their ㄹ, so 멀다 becomes 머네요, never 멀네요. For a finished event, just move to the past: 왔네요 (oh, it came), 끝났네요 (it's over already).

title: Seeking Agreement
plainEnglish: Asks the listener to confirm or agree with something you already believe is true.
whenToUse: Use it when you're fairly sure of something and just want the other person to nod along — exactly English 'right?', 'isn't it?', 'don't you think?': 오늘 좀 춥지요? (it's a bit cold today, right?). It's perfect for small talk, checking shared plans (우리 내일 만나죠? = we're meeting tomorrow, right?), or softening a statement into something collaborative. In speech it almost always contracts to 죠. Beyond questions, a falling-tone 지요/죠 can also gently confirm or explain ('그럼요, 좋죠' = sure, that works), but for beginners its core job is 'seeking agreement'. For a past fact you assume is shared, use 았/었지요: 어제 재미있었죠? (yesterday was fun, wasn't it?).
attachmentRule: Attach 지요 directly to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel harmony (춥다→춥지요, 가다→가지요, 좋다→좋지요). It commonly contracts to 죠 in speech (춥죠?). For past confirmation use 았/었지요 (갔지요?, 먹었지요?). With nouns use 이지요/지요 (학생이지요?).
contrastWith: Don't confuse the agreement-seeking A/V-지요? with a genuine yes-no question A/V-아/어요?. 학생이에요? truly asks because you don't know ('Are you a student?'), while 학생이지요? assumes you already believe it and just wants a nod ('You're a student, right?'). Use 아/어요? for real unknowns and 지요? only when you expect agreement. Also separate it from the discovery ending -네요: 춥네요 = 'oh, it's cold (I just noticed)', whereas 춥지요? = 'it's cold, isn't it? (you feel it too, right?)'. One is your fresh reaction; the other invites the listener's confirmation.

examples.en: It's cold, isn't it?
This movie is really fun, right?

examples.ko: 한국 음식 좋아하시죠? 그럼 같이 먹으러 가요.
examples.en: You like Korean food, right? Then let's go eat together.
We're meeting at 10 tomorrow, right?

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before 지요: ❌좋아지요 / ❌먹어지요. Why: 지요 attaches to the plain stem with no 아/어 → ✅좋지요, ✅먹지요. (Note ❌좋아지요 also collides with a different grammar, 좋아지다 = 'become good', so this error can change the meaning.)

Using 지요? for information you genuinely don't know: asking a stranger their name with ...지요? as if confirming. Why: 지요? presumes a shared answer and can sound oddly assuming; for a real question use ✅아/어요? (이름이 뭐예요?).
Forgetting the past form for past confirmation: ❌어제 재미있지요? to mean 'was it fun yesterday?'. Why: confirm a past fact with 았/었 → ✅어제 재미있었지요? / 재미있었죠?
studyOrder: Find the plain stem by dropping 다
Attach 지요 with no vowel change
Contract to 죠 in casual speech
Use 았/었지요 to confirm a past fact
beginnerExplanation: A/V-지요? is how Korean says 'right?' or 'isn't it?', and you pull it out when you're already pretty sure and simply want the listener to agree with you. The build is easy: attach 지요 straight onto the stem with no vowel harmony, so 춥다→춥지요? (it's cold, right?) and 가다→가지요?. In real speech it shrinks almost every time to 죠 — 춥죠?, 가죠? — so train your ear for that contracted form. The key feeling is *shared* knowledge: it's warm and inclusive, like reaching out for a 'yeah, totally' rather than truly questioning, which is why it's everywhere in friendly small talk. The main pitfall is reaching for it when you actually don't know the answer; for a real question, drop back to a plain 아/어요?. And to confirm something in the past, use 았/었죠? (좋았죠? = it was good, wasn't it?).

title: Subject Honorific
plainEnglish: Raises and respects the person who is doing the action, usually someone older or senior.
whenToUse: Use it whenever the *doer* of the action deserves respect — a teacher, grandparent, boss, customer, or any elder: 선생님이 가세요 (the teacher is going). It marks respect for the subject, separately from how polite you are to your *listener*. So you'd say it about a respected person even to a friend: 할머니가 주무세요 (grandma's sleeping). Crucially, you do *not* use it about yourself — 저는 가세요 is wrong; you only honor others. It also rides along in questions to be polite to the person you're addressing: 어디 가세요? (where are you going?), 뭐 드세요? (what are you having?). Pair it with honorific nouns/particles where they exist (진지 for 밥, 께서 for 이/가) in careful speech.
attachmentRule: After a vowel-ending stem add 시 (가다→가시다→가세요); after a consonant-ending stem add 으시 (받다→받으시다→받으세요). ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ then add 시 (살다→사시다→사세요). Some verbs are suppletive and change the whole word: 먹다/마시다→드시다 (드세요), 자다→주무시다, 있다→계시다, 말하다→말씀하시다.
contrastWith: Don't confuse subject-honorific -(으)시- (respect the *doer*) with listener-politeness like -요/-습니다 (respect the *person you're talking to*). 먹어요 is polite to your listener but says nothing special about the eater; 드세요 lifts the eater themselves. You can mix them freely: to a stranger, about yourself, 저는 밥을 먹어요 (polite, no 시 — you don't honor yourself); about their grandmother, 할머니께서 진지를 드세요 (honor the subject). Also note the suppletive swaps: ❌먹으세요 for an elder eating is grammatically formed but unnatural — use ✅드세요. And 있다 splits by meaning: 'exist/stay' → 계시다 (집에 계세요), but 'have/possess' → 있으시다 (시간이 있으세요?).

examples.en: Where are you going?
Grandfather is eating his meal now.

examples.ko: 어머니께서는 지금 집에 안 계셔서 나중에 다시 전화드릴게요.
examples.en: My mother isn't home right now, so I'll call again later.
The boss is reading the newspaper.

commonMistakes: Adding 시 to a plain verb instead of using the suppletive form: ❌선생님이 먹으세요. Why: high-frequency verbs replace the whole word → ✅드세요 (eat), ✅주무세요 (sleep), ✅계세요 (be present). Memorize the swap set.
Dropping 으 after a consonant stem: ❌받세요 / ❌읽세요. Why: a consonant stem needs the 으 bridge → ✅받으세요, ✅읽으세요. Vowel stems skip it (가세요).
Honoring yourself: ❌저는 가세요 / ❌제가 드세요. Why: -(으)시- elevates *others*, never the speaker → ✅저는 가요, ✅제가 먹어요.
studyOrder: Decide if the subject deserves respect
Add 시 after a vowel or 으시 after a consonant
Replace suppletive verbs like 먹다 with 드시다
Combine into the polite form, for example 가세요
beginnerExplanation: The honorific infix -(으)시- is the dial Korean uses to show respect to the *person doing the action* — essential for talking about elders, teachers, bosses, and customers. The mechanics mirror other endings: add 시 after a vowel stem and 으시 after a consonant stem, which surface in the polite present as 가세요 (가다) and 받으세요 (받다). Two big ideas keep you safe. First, this honors *others, never yourself* — say 저는 가요 about your own going, but 선생님이 가세요 about the teacher's. Second, a small club of everyday verbs don't just bolt on 시 — they transform entirely: 먹다/마시다→드시다 (드세요), 자다→주무시다 (주무세요), 있다→계시다 (계세요), 말하다→말씀하시다. These you simply memorize. The most common beginner slip is using a plain verb like 먹어요 about a respected person; with elders, reach for 드세요 instead.

title: Past Experience
plainEnglish: Says whether you have or have not ever done something before.
whenToUse: Use it to talk about life experience — whether something has *ever* happened, with no particular time attached, exactly like English 'have you ever...': 한국에 가 본 적 있어요? (have you ever been to Korea?). Choose 있어요 if you have done it, 없어요 if you never have: 한복을 입은 적 없어요 (I've never worn a hanbok). The noun 적 means 'a time/occasion', so you're literally saying 'there exists/doesn't exist a time when I did it'. It pairs constantly with 아/어 보다 to give the natural V-아/어 본 적 있다 ('have tried doing'), which softens questions about experience. Reserve it for the general 'ever/never' sense; if you mean one specific event at a known time, use the plain past instead.
attachmentRule: Make the past modifier on the stem: after a vowel-ending stem add ㄴ 적 (가다→간 적), after a consonant-ending stem add 은 적 (먹다→먹은 적). Then add 있어요 for have done or 없어요 for have never done. ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ then add ㄴ (살다→산 적); ㄷ irregular 듣다→들은 적; it often pairs with 아/어 보다 as V-아/어 본 적 있다.
contrastWith: Don't confuse experiential V-(으)ㄴ 적 있다 with the plain past V-았/었어요. 어제 김치를 먹었어요 reports one finished event at a specific time (I ate kimchi yesterday), while 김치를 먹은 적 있어요 says only that it has happened *at some point ever* (I've eaten kimchi before). Use the plain past for 'when' and the experience form for 'ever/never'. Also mind the modifier inside it: it must be the *past* modifier -(으)ㄴ, not the present -는. 가는 적 있어요 is wrong; the experience is completed, so it's 간 적 있어요. And note the verb 'do' for experience is 있다/없다 ('exist'), not 하다.

examples.en: Have you ever eaten kimchi?
I've never worn a hanbok.

examples.ko: 그 노래를 한 번 들은 적 있는데 제목이 기억 안 나요.
examples.en: I've heard that song once, but I can't remember the title.
Have you ever been to Korea?

commonMistakes: Using the present modifier instead of the past one: ❌가는 적 있어요 / ❌먹는 적 있어요. Why: the experience is finished, so it needs the past modifier → ✅간 적 있어요, ✅먹은 적 있어요.
Dropping 은 after a consonant stem: ❌먹ㄴ 적 / ❌먹은적 written wrong. Why: a consonant stem takes 은 (and 적 is a separate word) → ✅먹은 적 있어요. Vowel stems take bare ㄴ (간 적).
Using 하다 instead of 있다/없다: ❌가 본 적 했어요. Why: experience 'exists' or 'doesn't', so the verb is 있다/없다 → ✅가 본 적 있어요 / ✅가 본 적 없어요.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Add ㄴ 적 after a vowel or 은 적 after a consonant
Add 있어요 for have done or 없어요 for never
Optionally combine with 아/어 본 적 있다
beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 적 있다/없다 is Korean's 'have you ever...', used for life experience with no specific time pinned to it. Build it in two moves. First make the *past modifier* on the verb — ㄴ 적 after a vowel stem, 은 적 after a consonant stem — so 가다→간 적 and 먹다→먹은 적; the word 적 means 'an occasion/time'. Then close with 있어요 ('there is such a time' = I have) or 없어요 ('there isn't' = I never have): 한복을 입은 적 없어요 = 'I've never worn a hanbok'. A useful image: you're checking whether a memory-slot exists. It teams up beautifully with 아/어 보다 to make V-아/어 본 적 있다, the smooth, natural way to ask 'have you ever tried...' (가 본 적 있어요?). The biggest trap is grabbing the present modifier 가는 적 — the experience is done, so it must be the past modifier 간 적.
